title: Jensen Theory and Nevanlinna's First Main Theorem

items.title: Poisson–Jensen formula for a meromorphic function on a disc
items.statement: For nonzero meromorphic f on a neighbourhood of the closed radius-R disc, and no zero or pole on its boundary, log|f(z)| at each interior point away from its divisor equals the Poisson average of boundary log|f| minus the sum of disc Green kernels G_R(z,a) over zeros plus the sum over poles, with multiplicity; G_R(z,a)=log|(R²-conj(a)z)/(R(z-a))|. At a boundary-divisor radius the identity is the limit through regular radii.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: On a regular closed disc list its finite divisor. For each a construct B_a(z)=R(z-a)/(R²-conj(a)z), analytic on a neighbourhood of the closed disc, modulus one on the circle and with exactly one interior zero. Multiply f by the pole factors and divide by the zero factors with multiplicity; local zero/pole factorisation makes the resulting g holomorphic and nowhere zero on a neighbourhood of the closed disc. Locally expand log(g/g(z0)) where it is close to 1, so log|g| is harmonic; apply the published Poisson representation. On the boundary |B_a|=1, and solving for log|f| gives the displayed Green signs. For a boundary divisor, use regular radii tending to R and prove local logarithmic singularities are integrable in angle; the same limit holds at each fixed interior z.

items.title: Counting, chordal proximity and characteristic of a meromorphic function
items.statement: For non-identically-infinity meromorphic f on C and a target a for which f is not identically a, n(r,a;f) counts a-points in |z|≤r with local multiplicity (poles when a=∞); N(r,a)=n(0,a)log r+∫₀ʳ(n(t,a)-n(0,a))dt/t. Set δ(w,a)=|w-a|/(sqrt(1+|w|²)sqrt(1+|a|²)) for finite w,a, δ(w,∞)=1/sqrt(1+|w|²), with continuous endpoint values. Define m(r,a;f)=(2π)⁻¹∫log(1/δ(f(re^{it}),a))dt and T(r,f)=m(r,∞;f)+N(r,∞;f). The normalized chordal sphere has diameter one; this δ is one half the chord length for unit-sphere stereographic projection.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.strategy: Fix the closed-disc counting convention, multiplicity, central correction, ∞ target and normalized chordal formula explicitly. Circle singularities are improper Lebesgue integrals proved finite in the next item; finite constant maps retain T, but the identically attained target is excluded from n and m. The coordinate formula is stipulated locally, so no unlisted Riemann-sphere page result is used as a proof premise.

items.title: Well-definedness and radius conventions for Nevanlinna quantities
items.statement: For every allowed (f,a) the counts on bounded discs are finite, N(r,a) and m(r,a) are finite and continuous for r>0 even at a divisor radius, and a=∞ counts precisely poles. If N_{r0}(r,a)=∫_{r0}^r n(t,a)dt/t, then N_{r0}(r,a)=N(r,a)-N(r0,a) for r,r0>0, so the corresponding characteristic changes by exactly the constant -N(r0,∞). Proximity alone need not be monotone.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: On each compact disc the a-divisor is finite by isolated zeros/poles. Factor f-a (or 1/f at a pole) near each circle intersection; log inverse chordal distance is an integer multiple of -log|re^{it}-b| plus a continuous bounded remainder. The angular logarithm is locally integrable and its mean is continuous in r, including r=|b|, by splitting a small angular arc and estimating ∫|log sqrt((r-|b|)²+cθ²)|dθ uniformly. N is an explicit finite sum of log(r/|b|) for 0<|b|≤r plus n(0,a)log r; each new term is zero at entry radius. Split the defining integral at r0 to prove the exact base-change constant.

items.title: Meromorphic Jensen identity with a zero or pole at the centre
items.statement: For finite a and nonconstant meromorphic f, write f(z)-a=c_a z^{k_a}+ higher Laurent terms near 0 with c_a≠0 and k_a∈Z. For every r>0, M_r log|f-a|=log|c_a|+N(r,a;f)-N(r,∞;f), where M_r is the angular mean and a divisor on |z|=r is interpreted by continuous radial limit.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: Apply Poisson–Jensen to f-a on a regular radius and let z→0. Separate any central factor c_a z^{k_a}; each noncentral zero contributes log(r/|b|) and each pole the opposite sign. The central term k_a log r cancels against n(0,a)log r-n(0,∞)log r by the Laurent order identity. Reassemble exactly N(r,a)-N(r,∞), retaining log|c_a|, including f(0)=a and f(0)=∞. Extend from regular radii using the preceding continuity result.

items.title: Ahlfors–Shimizu area form of the characteristic
items.statement: For nonconstant meromorphic f, its spherical derivative f#=|f′|/(1+|f|²), continuously extended at poles, gives A(r,f)=π⁻¹∫_{|z|≤r}(f#)²dA and T_AS(r,f)=∫₀ʳ A(t,f)dt/t. Then T(r,f)=T_AS(r,f)+C∞(f), where C∞=½log(1+|f(0)|²) if f(0) is finite and C∞=log|c| if f(z)=c z^{-m}+… at 0. Thus T_AS is finite, nondecreasing, and convex in log r.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: Set u=½log(1+|f|²). Away from poles calculate Δu=2(f#)² by Cauchy–Riemann. At a pole p of order m, u+m log|z-p|=½log(|(z-p)^m|²+|h(z)|²) with h=(z-p)^mf holomorphic and nonzero, so this correction is C²; f#² extends continuously. On a fixed regular disc add the finitely many m log|z-p| corrections to obtain a C² function. For its circular mean U(r), prove (rU′)′=r M_r(Δu) by the polar Laplacian and the vanishing angular second-derivative integral. Integrate from 0 twice, with the explicit mean of log|z-p| equal to log max(r,|p|), then identify the finite pole terms with N(r,∞). The small-r limit gives the stated centre constant, including a centre pole. Continuity extends across divisor radii.

items.title: Nevanlinna’s First Main Theorem with exact centre constant
items.statement: For nonconstant meromorphic f:C→Ĉ and each fixed a∈Ĉ, m(r,a;f)+N(r,a;f)=T(r,f)+C(f,a) for every r>0. For finite a, C(f,a)=½log(1+|a|²)-log|c_a| with c_a the first nonzero Laurent coefficient of f-a at 0; for a=∞, C(f,∞)=0. In particular the difference is O_{f,a}(1) as r→∞.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: For finite a use the pointwise normalized chordal identity log(1/δ(f,a))=½log(1+|f|²)+½log(1+|a|²)-log|f-a|, valid away from isolated poles and a-points and integrable through them. Average it, subtract the ∞ proximity, and insert the centre Jensen identity. This yields the explicit constant, including f(0)=a and f(0)=∞. At a=∞ the equation is the definition of T. No analogy substitutes for the ∞ case.

items.title: Elementary characteristic laws and fixed rational composition
items.statement: For meromorphic f,g (where the displayed expressions are meromorphic), as r→∞: T(r,fg)≤T(r,f)+T(r,g)+O(1), T(r,f+g)≤T(r,f)+T(r,g)+O(1), T(r,1/f)=T(r,f)+O_f(1) when f is not identically zero, and T(r,R(f))=(deg R)T(r,f)+O_{R,f}(1) for a fixed rational map R of degree max(deg P,deg Q) in coprime form and nonconstant f. Degree-zero constant maps have bounded characteristic.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: Compare chordal T with T0=m0+N∞ using 0≤½log(1+|w|²)-log+|w|≤½log2. Pointwise logarithmic inequalities and local pole-order bounds prove product and sum laws for r≥1. The First Main Theorem at target 0 proves inversion up to its fixed centre constant. For polynomial P of degree p, log+|P(w)|=p log+|w|+O_P(1) uniformly; its pole orders multiply by p. For R=P/Q, reciprocal and target translation reduce to deg Q=d>deg P. On neighborhoods of the finitely many zeros of Q, coprimality bounds |P| above and below; on the compact complement including infinity, R and 1/Q are bounded. Splitting the circular mean gives m0(R(f))=m0(1/Q(f))+O_R(1), and their pole divisors coincide. Apply polynomial and reciprocal laws, then transfer back to chordal T. The normalized positive-degree denominator has a nonempty zero set by the declared fundamental theorem of algebra.

items.title: Order and lower order from the Nevanlinna characteristic
items.statement: For nonconstant meromorphic f define ρ(f)=limsup_{r→∞}(log T(r,f))/log r and λ(f)=liminf of the same ratio, for all sufficiently large r>1 with T(r,f)>1; the First Main Theorem ensures this range exists. Both lie in [0,∞], and finite order means ρ<∞. Constant finite maps have upper and lower order zero by convention. For an entire f the classical maximum-modulus order is addressed by the next proposition, while meromorphic growth is defined by T rather than a pole-infinite maximum modulus.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.strategy: The First Main Theorem at a=f(0), or at a=∞ when the centre is a pole, gives T(r,f)≥log r+O(1) for a nonconstant map, so log T is eventually defined. The area identity gives monotonicity after subtracting a fixed centre constant and shows the limits are stable under the bounded normalization change. Distinguish this from log log maximum modulus, which is only an entire-function expression.

items.title: Entire-function order agrees with maximum-modulus order
items.statement: For a nonconstant entire function f, define M(r,f)=max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|, m₀(r,f)=(2π)⁻¹∫₀²π log⁺|f(re^{it})|dt, and T₀(r,f)=m₀(r,f)+N(r,∞;f)=m₀(r,f). For every 0<r<R, T₀(r,f)≤log⁺M(r,f)≤((R+r)/(R-r))T₀(R,f). Consequently its Nevanlinna order ρ(f) and lower order λ(f) agree with limsup and liminf of log(log⁺M(r,f))/log r, taken for all sufficiently large r with log⁺M(r,f)>1.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: Define T0=m0+N∞ and compare it uniformly with chordal T. The lower bound is pointwise. For the upper bound, apply Poisson–Jensen on radius R at every nonzero value on the inner circle, prove the zero Green terms are nonnegative, bound the Poisson kernel by (R+r)/(R-r), and replace boundary log|f| by log+|f| before taking the supremum. Taylor expansion and Cauchy coefficient estimates show log+ M(r)>1 eventually. Set R=2r; the two inequalities squeeze both logarithmic limits, while the bounded T−T0 difference and fixed radius dilation preserve limsup and liminf. Select the first nonzero positive Taylor index by the declared well-ordering principle.

items.title: Rational functions are exactly those with logarithmic characteristic
items.statement: A nonconstant meromorphic f on C is rational if and only if T(r,f)=O(log r) as r→∞. More precisely, a rational map of degree d has T(r,f)=d log r+O(1).

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: Forward: compute T(r,z)=½log(1+r²)=log r+O(1) and apply the fixed rational composition law to the rational map f. Reverse: because chordal proximity is nonnegative, N(r,∞)≤T(r,f)≤C log r for r≥r0. If there were infinitely many poles, fix an integer M>C and choose a finite list of M poles, with r_M≥1 containing them; the integrated-count formula gives N(R,∞)≥M log R−C_M for R≥r_M, contradicting the uniform bound as R→∞. Thus the pole set is finite. Let q(z)=∏(z−p)^{m_p}, with the empty product 1, and g=qf; pole characterization shows g is entire. Direct polynomial growth gives T(r,q)=O(log r); the product law gives T(r,g)=O(log r), hence T0(r,g)≤T(r,g)=O(log r). If g is constant, f=g/q is rational. Otherwise the entire maximum-modulus inequality with R=2r gives log+M(r,g)≤3T0(2r,g)=O(log r), hence M(r,g)≤C1r^K for some K≥0. Cauchy coefficient bounds make every Taylor coefficient of degree n>K vanish; the entire Taylor expansion then makes g a polynomial, so f=g/q is rational. Use only a finite pole list and no AC. The authored threshold-radius selection uses the declared well-ordering principle on natural numbers.

title: Jensen Theory and Nevanlinna's First Main Theorem: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A repeated zero contributes its Green kernel twice
items.statement: For f(z)=(z-b)² with 0<|b|<R and |z|<R, the radius-R Poisson–Jensen identity has the term -2G_R(z,b), and at z=0 the Jensen correction is 2log(R/|b|).

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: The zero b has multiplicity two and there are no poles. On the boundary log|f|=2log|Re^{it}-b|. The Poisson average is twice the harmonic extension of log|Re^{it}-b|; subtract twice the explicit Green kernel. Evaluate at the centre to display the factor two.

items.title: A centre a-point requires regularised counting
items.statement: For a,c∈C, an integer m≥1, c≠0, and f(z)=a+cz^m, every r>0 has n(0,a;f)=m and N(r,a;f)=m log r, while ∫₀ʳ n(t,a;f)dt/t diverges. The centre Jensen mean is log|c|+m log r, and the exact First Main Theorem constant is ½log(1+|a|²)−log|c|; log|f(0)−a| is not finite.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: Count the order-m zero at 0 for every positive radius. Insert n(t,a)-m=0 into the regularized formula, and evaluate the boundary mean log|f-a|=log|c|+m log r. Check the explicit constant C(f,a)=½log(1+|a|²)-log|c|, showing why a naive log|f(0)-a| is invalid.

items.title: Characteristics of a monomial, an exponential and a tangent
items.statement: For d≥1, T(r,z^d)=d log r+O(1); T(r,e^z)=r/π+O(1); and T(r,tan z)=2r/π+O(1), all with the normalized chordal characteristic. Their meromorphic orders are respectively 0, 1 and 1.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: For z^d compute T exactly from its chordal mean and absence of poles. For exp(z), use the complex exponential modulus and Euler's formula to obtain log+|exp(re^{it})|=(r cos t)+; evaluate its integral from the sine/cosine signs, quarter-turn values, derivative, and FTC. For complex tan z, use the complex exponential definitions of sine and cosine and exp addition to derive tan z=-i(E-1)/(E+1), E=exp(2iz); verify E is nonconstant, compute log+|E(re^{it})|=(-2r sin t)+ and its angular integral, then apply the degree-one fixed-rational composition law. For each entire function T differs from the log-plus mean by at most ½log2. Take log T/log r for the three orders.

items.title: Characteristic under a target Möbius change
items.statement: For nonconstant meromorphic f and a∈C, M_a(w)=(1+conj(a)w)/(w-a) is degree one and T(r,M_a∘f)=T(r,f)+O_{f,a}(1); moreover the normalized chordal proximity to a equals the proximity to ∞ after M_a.

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: Write M_a(w)=conjugate(a)+(1+|a|²)/(w-a) and verify its determinant is nonzero. The algebraic identity |1+conjugate(a)w|²+|w-a|²=(1+|a|²)(1+|w|²) gives δ(M_a(w),∞)=δ(w,a) at every sphere point, including both endpoints. Locally, zero factorization shows an a-point of f of order m becomes a pole of M_a(f) of order m; pole characterization shows a pole of f is sent to the finite value conjugate(a). Thus the infinity divisor of the composition is exactly the a-divisor of f. Apply the degree-one rational characteristic law and the First Main Theorem for the exact target sum.

items.title: Reciprocal Gamma has order one and characteristic of size r log r
items.statement: For the published reciprocal Gamma function, T(r,1/Γ)=Θ(r log r) as r→∞; hence its Nevanlinna order and lower order are both one. Its zeros are exactly 0,-1,-2,… and it has no poles.

references.title: Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 2 §5, reciprocal-Gamma exercise, printed pp.80–81
K. Chandrasekharan, Lectures on the Riemann Zeta-Function, Lecture 7 §6, Stirling formula, printed pp.60–62

items.proof_strategy: Use the locally uniform Weierstrass product to identify the entire reciprocal and its simple zero set. For |z|=r, split factors at n≤2r and n>2r: the finite part is O(r log r), while the quadratic logarithm bound makes the tail O(r), giving a pointwise log+ bound whose circular mean is O(r log r). For the lower bound choose δ=π/4 in the published sectorial Stirling statement and integrate over the fixed arc 2π/3≤arg z≤3π/4; its hypotheses include the closed arc and give log|1/Γ(re^{it})|≥c r log r uniformly there. The angular log-plus mean is therefore Ω(r log r). Since the reciprocal is entire, the chordal characteristic differs from this mean by at most 1/2 log 2; the two bounds imply T=Θ(r log r) and both orders equal one. The B page requires the Gamma page in both the run manifest and plan spec; use its product, continuation, and Stirling claims with their exact hypotheses, and independently report the proof-step gap in the published Stirling item.

items.title: Rational degree appears as logarithmic characteristic
items.statement: For R(z)=(z²+1)/(z-1), which has degree two, T(r,R)=2log r+O(1). For r>1 its pole count contributes N(r,∞)=log r and its boundary proximity contributes log r+O(1).

references.title: Alexandre Eremenko, Lectures on Nevanlinna Theory, §§1–3
Goldberg–Ostrovskii, Value Distribution of Meromorphic Functions, Ch. 1 §§1–2,4,6–7; Ch. 2 §1

items.proof_strategy: The numerator and denominator are coprime, so R has degree two. Apply rational composition to z. Directly, R has one simple pole at 1 and N∞=log r for r>1. Uniformly on |z|=r≫1, R(z)=z+1+2/(z-1), so log(1/δ(R(z),∞))=log r+O(1) after angular averaging. Add the terms.
